newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-UDINESE? TRY THE BARGAIN BASEMENT.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-UDINESE? TRY THE BARGAIN BASEMENT.

text.p: In the great department store of Italian soccer, AC Milan and Juventus prefer to make their purchases at the luxury goods counter.
Udinese, on the other hand, are far more likely to be sniffing around in the bargain basement.
Or the local reject shop.
The provincial north-eastern club, regularly in and out of serie A in recent years, have the sort of canny reputation that would make any bargain-hunter glow with pride.
With an eagle eye for detecting and then polishing gems where others see only dull stones, Udinese have this season turned out a team who have humbled the big spenders.
In the space of a week they beat league leaders and European Cup holders Juventus 3-0 in Turin after playing for 87 minutes with only 10-men and then travelled to second-placed Parma for a 2-0 win.
"In Friuli they know how to invest in goals," commented an admiring Gazzetta dello Sport, referring to the northeast region, after Udinese's win in Turin.
They are seventh in the league and possibly heading for their best finish since fourth place in 1956-57.
Their most recent best finish was sixth in 1983, the season before they signed Brazilian Zico from Flamengo for around $4 million.
The hero against Parma was goalkeeper Massimiliano Caniato, paid more than a shop assistant but still getting by on Italian soccer's minimum monthly wage of about $1,600.
Until recently the 29-year-old had wondered whether he still had a future in top-level soccer.

Instead Udinese's unheralded and unknown third-choice 'keeper suddenly found himself in goal after Graziano Battistini, himself signed from third division Alessandria in 1993, was sidelined and reserve Luigi Turci was injured.
Caniato played the game of his life, getting the highest rating of the day in at least one newspaper.
The first goal was scored by 24-year-old Alessandro Pierini, his first in serie A.
The second was a penalty by Oliver Bierhoff.
The German international striker, scorer of the goals that gave his country the European championship last summer and valued at around $9 million, may not appear to fit the mold of a cheap castoff.
But when Udinese bought him in 1995 for around $1.2 million his career had appeared to be heading nowhere.
Regarded for years by Germans as a loser because he lacked mobility and speed, Bierhoff was transformed at Udinese within a year of joining into a first-choice international.
Between 1985 and 1990, he had bounced about between Bundesliga teams Bayer Uerdingen, Hamburg and Borussia Moenchengladbach, spending most of his time on the bench.
He moved to Austria and then in June 1991, Internazionale Milan signed him to disbelief in Germany.
However Inter then loaned him to Ascoli where he had a nightmare start and saw his team relegated.
That is when he started scoring goals and when Udinese first scented a whiff of some cut-price quality.
Bierhoff, 28, now plans to stay at Udinese.
"There are not many clubs that want me there," he said of his homeland earlier this month.

Bierhoff also scored against Juventus but the two-goal hero there was Brazilian Marcio Amoroso, a player similar to Barcelona's Ronaldo in many respects other than the fact that he is paid a tiny fraction of his compatriot's wages.
Like the great Zico, whom Udinese signed after the Brazilian had been laid off by injury for several months, Amoroso also came from Flamengo via the local hospital.

Amoroso had been joint top goalscorer in Brazil with Guarani 1994 when he scored 19 goals in 26 games. He was seen as the next big Brazilian name with coach Mario Zagallo reportedly saying "For me, Brazil is him and 10 players."
Then he hurt his knee. From being prized at around $18 million, Amoroso found himself facing an eight-month layoff with no guarantee of a successful comeback and his value sank.
Enter Udinese. The club picked him up for around $4.2 million and this season he has scored 10 league goals, the same as Bierhoff, and signed a new contract to stay.
Old Udinese watchers are not surprised.
The club also launched the career in Italy of Argentine Abel Balbo, bringing him over from River Plate in 1989 when his career was just starting out.
Balbo scored 65 goals in 134 league matches for Udinese and then left for Roma in 1993.
Udinese, need it be said, made a tidy profit.
"It's your fault," Roma owner Franco Sensi told reporters at the time when negotiations were underway.
"You wrote that Balbo was ours and the Udinese directors immediately took the chance to put the price up."
